summary: Refunded tickets still admit at an OFFLINE gate — revocation does not reach scanners
description:
Found by the TKT-157 adversarial review (finding F1, accepted as a real gap and rejected as a change to that ticket).

TKT-157 refuses a refunded ticket at a **live** gate. An **offline** scanner has no way to learn a ticket was refunded, so it admits the holder, and `ReconcileAdmission` then faithfully records that admission — `entry`/`redeemed`/`duplicate_admit` appended after the refund, with a chain that verifies clean and proves a refunded ticket was used.

**Blocking reconciliation is the wrong fix and was rejected on those grounds.** The person is already inside; refusing to record it would falsify the trail rather than protect a gate (ADR-038 §4). The missing capability is **revocation propagation to scanners** — a scanner/offline-distribution feature in ADR-025's territory.

Also considered and rejected for TKT-157: raising an integrity alarm on reconciling a refunded ticket. `oweAlarm` writes to the **integrity** alarm channel, which means *the chain is suspect*; a refunded-but-admitted ticket is not an integrity event, and TKT-147 is already open to replace that channel's free-text reason with fixed reason codes. Overloading it now would make TKT-147 worse.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- [ ] A scanner that went offline before a refund, and syncs after it, does not admit the refunded holder — or, if it already did, the operator is told through a channel that means *this* rather than *the chain is suspect*.
- [ ] Whatever the mechanism, reconciliation still records what physically happened. An occurrence is never dropped to make the trail look better.
- [ ] The revocation feed is bounded and testable offline (no live-network assumption at a gate).

Quality gates: `make check` green; `access verify-lifecycle` green; contract tests.

binding.rule: Money is integer minor units + ISO currency code — floats are banned on money paths.

Traceability is a must, for money and tickets: money-relevant records land as immutable, hash-chained, signed journal entries from the first order (corrections = compensating entries; read models = projections), and every ticket/entitlement state change (issued, delivered, transferred, resold, exchanged, redeemed, reissued, invalidated) is an append-only lifecycle event linked to its order.

governingAdrs.why: Every lifecycle event goes through store.appendLifecycle — the verifier asserts one-to-one coverage, so a direct INSERT into lifecycle_events reads as tampering and fails `access verify-lifecycle` in the gate. Canonical forms are pinned by golden literals; changing a byte is a canonical-version migration, not a test update. Also: name the adversary before writing 'tamper-evident'.

Inventory's claim transaction is the contention path. Giving capacity back must go through the same row-locked transaction discipline; a plain UPDATE outside it can drive confirmed_quantity negative or double-return under concurrency.
Capacity adjustments clamp rather than reject. Returning capacity must not let availability exceed the pool's capacity, and the clamp reasoning is the precedent for what to do when it would.

Corrections are COMPENSATING ENTRIES, never mutations. A refund/exchange appends a new signed fact; the original sale fact and its hash link are untouched. The payments journal has a DB trigger that raises on UPDATE/DELETE — any design that 'adjusts' a fact is rejected by the database, not by review.

If any domain event payload changes or a new one is published: bump on CONSUMER SEMANTICS, not parse compatibility, and consumers dispatch on `schema` BEFORE decoding `data`. A fixture built from the type under test cannot fail.

Fail closed. Responses are validated against the spec; an undeclared status code becomes a 500. Every new endpoint must declare every status it can answer, and a downstream answer commerce cannot validate aborts rather than degrades.

Contract-first. A new operation is written in the service's openapi.yaml first, then `openapi_gen.go` / `api-types.gen.ts` are regenerated and COMMITTED before the gate runs — check-generate diffs against HEAD, so an uncommitted regen reads as drift.
Commerce and inventory ARE inside the smoke happy-path coverage gate. A new documented 2xx operation must be exercised through the running stack or the suite fails.

Migrations run out-of-band via each binary's `migrate` subcommand as a one-shot Compose job. Add the SQL under the service's internal/store/migrations/ with the next number; the server path never migrates.

governingTests.why: EVERY migration in this service carries a FOUR-TEST SET, enforced by convention and by a live tripwire: statement-order, schema, representative-volume, and irreversibility (TestRepeatableAdmissionMigrationIsIrreversible and siblings). 0009's own Down block RAISEs deliberately and its comment names those tests as the reason. A new migration that ships a working rollback is caught here, not in review — and this is discoverable only by failing the gate, which is exactly the class shaping.md says to surface now.

TestRefundedRefusalPrecedesIntegrityFailOpen pins ADR-038 §4's ORDERING — the refunded check runs before verifyTicketChain. Any change to the admission decision path that reorders those two goes red here. TestScanOfRefundedTicketIsRefused pins the live half this ticket must not regress.

`access verify-lifecycle` runs inside the gate's smoke suite AND the suite deliberately CORRUPTS the trail to assert the verifier REFUSES (502-507). A new lifecycle event type or any direct INSERT into lifecycle_events reads as tampering and fails here — which is the enforcement behind ADR-021's appendLifecycle rule.

A new documented 2xx operation MUST be exercised through the running stack or the smoke coverage gate fails. A revocation-feed endpoint therefore needs a smoke exercise in the same PR, not a follow-up — and openapi_gen.go must be regenerated AND COMMITTED before the gate runs, since check-generate diffs against HEAD.

objective.note: A refunded ticket that still opens an offline gate is a real revenue and access-control hole; TKT-157 closed only the live half and ADR-038 §4 says so explicitly.

scope.note: MECHANISM IS NO LONGER OPEN — the code narrowed it to one option since this note was written (2026-07-31). Verified at HEAD: (a) short-TTL credentials are DEAD — the QR credential carries no expiry at all, only `iat` (services/access/internal/ticket/token.go:14-21), so a TTL means rolling reissue of every ticket QR plus a redelivery path to every buyer — a different epic, not this ticket; (b) an online check with offline grace contradicts this ticket's own AC3 and ADR-025's offline posture; (c) a REVOCATION FEED pulled by the scanner is viable and cheap today, because the substrate already exists — enrolled per-device tokens with an authenticated, organizer-scoped channel (0009_scanner_devices.sql), a durable IndexedDB occurrence store and an `online` handler with a sync moment (web/scanner/src/App.tsx:106-200), and a QR carrying `tid` so a revoked-ticket match is a local set lookup with no extra decode. WHAT REMAINS FOR THE HUMAN IS NOT THE MECHANISM BUT THE STALENESS POLICY — see `uncertainties`. Scope OUT for this ticket regardless: seat/pass revocation semantics beyond refunded, hardware gates, and binding occurrence identity to a device (ADR-025 §D3 defers that separately).

uncertainties.note: THE ONE REAL DECISION, and it is a product call: how stale may a scanner's revocation view be, and what may a scanner do once it exceeds that? Three sub-questions, each with a different failure mode. (1) FEED FRESHNESS — how often does a connected scanner re-pull? (2) STALENESS CEILING — after how long without a successful pull is the view untrusted? (3) BEHAVIOUR AT THE CEILING — keep admitting on a stale list (fail OPEN: a refunded holder walks in, which is today's behaviour and the hole this ticket exists to close), or refuse (fail CLOSED: a connectivity outage turns away paying customers at a live turnstile). ADR-038 §4 already took the analogous call for a BROKEN CHAIN and chose fail-open-once, reasoning that denying a real customer at a turnstile is the worse failure — but it chose the opposite for a REFUNDED holder, on the grounds that they are not a real customer. That precedent points at fail-closed-on-stale, but it is the owner's to take because it trades revenue-at-the-gate against a customer-facing outage, and the acceptable ceiling depends on the venue's real connectivity, which engineering cannot read out of the code. NOTE the ticket's AC1 already offers a documented escape hatch — 'or, if it already did, the operator is told through a channel that means THIS' — and that channel already EXISTS: SubjectAdmissionConflictAlarm, `platform.access.admission-conflict.alarm` (services/access/internal/store/reconcile.go:18), a class deliberately separate from the integrity alarms. So a minimum-viable slice that alarms on reconciling a refunded ticket is available even if the ceiling decision is deferred — see `first_slice`.

dependencies.note: No OPEN blockers. TKT-157 (live refusal) is Done; TKT-19 is the parent epic and TKT-162 is currently its ONLY child, so no sibling scanner work is in flight to collide with. ADR-025 §D6 explicitly hands the scanner-side durability contract to TKT-19's design, which is this ticket's lineage — a licence, not a blocker.

approach.note: Blocked ONLY on the staleness decision in `uncertainties` — the mechanism itself is settled (see `scope`). Held at `owner: human` rather than `deferred` on purpose: shaping.md forbids `approach: deferred` when a ticket touches an AUTH surface, and a revocation feed is exactly that — it decides who gets through a door, it adds an organizer-scoped authenticated read, and the ceiling behaviour IS the trust boundary. TWO STRUCTURAL FACTS the drafter must not rediscover. (i) THERE IS NO REFUND EVENT TO TAP: the refund fact is written by a SYNCHRONOUS commerce -> access internal HTTP call (services/commerce/internal/refunds/service.go:105 -> services/access/internal/api/refunds.go:28 -> RefundOrderTickets), landing only as a `refunded` row in access's own lifecycle_events. No NATS subject carries a refund and no consumer subscribes to one, so the feed reads lifecycle_events directly — do NOT design around a refund event stream, it does not exist. (ii) ADR-025 HAS NO PROVISION FOR DISTRIBUTING TICKET STATE TO SCANNERS — its offline contract is entirely about RECORDING AFTER THE FACT. So this ticket is not merely implementing a decided ADR: pushing revocation state toward a gate is NEW decision territory and almost certainly needs its own ADR (staleness ceiling, fail-open-vs-closed, feed bounding, and the named adversary per ADR-021). Budget for authoring it. Direction once the call is made, verified against HEAD: a new organizer-scoped operation on services/access/api/openapi.yaml under ScannerDeviceToken (contract first per ADR-009, regenerate AND COMMIT openapi_gen.go before the gate — check-generate diffs against HEAD); serve refunded ticket ids for the device's organizer with a monotonic cursor so the feed is bounded and incremental; the scanner pulls on the same `online` edge that already drives sync and stores the set beside the occurrence queue; the offline admit decision consults it before opening. RECONCILIATION IS NOT TOUCHED — ADR-038 §4 and this ticket's AC2 both forbid dropping an occurrence to make the trail look better; if a stale scanner did admit, the fact is recorded and the operator learns it through the admission-conflict alarm, never by falsifying the trail.

first_slice.note: DECIDED 2026-08-22 (owner chose option B): Slice B was split out as TKT-269 (alarm on reconciling a refunded ticket — closes AC1's second branch, needs no product decision). TKT-162 RETAINS the feed: AC1's first branch (a scanner that synced after a refund does not admit the holder) and AC3 (a bounded, offline-testable revocation feed). That is this ticket's slice and it is well-defined; it is simply still gated on the staleness decision in `uncertainties`, which is why scope/approach/success stay open.

success.note: The three ACs on the ticket are sound and were re-read against HEAD — AC2 in particular is already protected by ADR-038 §4 and by TestRefundedEventsKeepTheLifecycleChainVerifiable. What cannot be written yet is the MEASURABLE form of AC1 and AC3, because both need a number the staleness decision supplies: AC1's 'does not admit' needs the ceiling behaviour to say what happens past it, and AC3's 'bounded' needs the freshness interval to be a testable bound rather than a word. Everything else is ready to write the moment that call lands.

context_memo.note: Baked and RE-VERIFIED at HEAD on 2026-08-22, not inherited on trust. All nine cited governingAdrs resolve to real files in docs/adr/. governingTests added — it was absent from the 2026-07-31 bake, and shaping.md requires it non-empty or explicitly none.

comments.body:
<!-- sdlc:stage=backlog kind=readiness -->
### ❌ Implementation readiness — FAIL (deliberately)

Not a defect: the mechanism is a product decision nobody has taken. Shaping starts with *how long may an offline scanner lag, and what may it do while lagging* — not with a plan. The board will refuse Gate 1 until that is answered, which is correct.

<!-- sdlc:stage=backlog kind=readiness -->
### ❌ Implementation readiness — still FAIL, but for a much smaller reason (re-shaped 2026-08-22)

The 2026-07-31 verdict was right to stop, and its framing is now **stale**. That note put the mechanism itself in question — "revocation list, short-TTL credentials, or an online check with an offline grace". Reading the code at HEAD closes two of those three, so the open question is narrower and sharper than it was.

**What the code decided while this ticket sat in Backlog**

- **Short-TTL credentials are dead.** The QR credential has no expiry field — `Claims` carries `iat` and nothing else (`services/access/internal/ticket/token.go:14-21`). A TTL means rolling reissue of every ticket QR plus a redelivery path to every buyer. That is an epic, not this ticket.
- **An online check with offline grace contradicts this ticket's own AC3** ("no live-network assumption at a gate") and ADR-025's offline posture.
- **A pulled revocation feed is viable and cheap**, because the substrate landed since shaping: enrolled per-device tokens giving an authenticated, organizer-scoped channel (`0009_scanner_devices.sql`), a durable IndexedDB occurrence store with an `online` handler and a sync moment (`web/scanner/src/App.tsx:106-200`), and a QR carrying `tid` so a revoked-ticket check is a local set lookup.

**The defect is confirmed, not just alleged.** `ReconcileAdmission` (`services/access/internal/store/reconcile.go:73`) never calls `ticketRefunded` — the guard TKT-157 added at `postgres.go:319` (and `scan.go:95` for passes) exists on the live paths only. An offline admit of a refunded ticket is recorded as an ordinary redemption and the chain verifies clean, exactly as the ticket says. An offline scanner today holds **no ticket state whatsoever** — only its IndexedDB occurrence queue — and no endpoint exists that would give it any.

**Two structural facts that change the shape of the work, and that a plan drafter would otherwise rediscover the hard way**

- **There is no refund event to subscribe to.** The refund fact is written by a *synchronous* commerce→access internal HTTP call (`services/commerce/internal/refunds/service.go:105` → `services/access/internal/api/refunds.go:28` → `RefundOrderTickets`), landing only as a `refunded` row in access's own `lifecycle_events`. No NATS subject carries a refund; no consumer subscribes to one. The feed must read `lifecycle_events` directly — any design premised on tapping a refund stream is designing around something that does not exist.
- **ADR-025 does not cover this.** Its offline contract is entirely about *recording after the fact*; it has no provision for distributing ticket state toward a gate. So TKT-162 is not "implement a decided ADR" — pushing revocation state to scanners is new decision territory and almost certainly needs **its own ADR** (staleness ceiling, fail-open vs fail-closed, feed bounding, named adversary per ADR-021). That should be budgeted into the plan, not discovered during it.

**What is actually still open — one product decision, three parts**

1. **Feed freshness** — how often does a connected scanner re-pull?
2. **Staleness ceiling** — after how long without a successful pull is the view untrusted?
3. **Behaviour at the ceiling** — keep admitting (**fail open**: a refunded holder walks in — today's behaviour, the hole this ticket exists to close) or refuse (**fail closed**: a connectivity outage turns away paying customers at a live turnstile).

This is not engineering hesitation. ADR-038 §4 already took the *analogous* call for a broken chain and chose fail-open-once — "denying a real customer at a live turnstile is the worse failure" — then chose the *opposite* for a refunded holder, because they are not a real customer. That precedent points at fail-closed-on-stale, but the acceptable ceiling depends on the venue's real connectivity, which is not readable from the code, and the trade is revenue-at-the-gate against a customer-facing outage. It is the owner's call.

**There is a no-decision slice available.** AC1 offers an explicit escape hatch — *"or, if it already did, the operator is told through a channel that means this rather than the chain is suspect"* — and that channel already exists: `SubjectAdmissionConflictAlarm` / `platform.access.admission-conflict.alarm` (`reconcile.go:18`), deliberately separate from the integrity class. **Slice B** (alarm on reconciling a refunded ticket) needs no product decision, closes AC1's second branch, and leaves AC2 intact because an alarm records rather than suppresses. It is a *separate ticket*, though — not a descope — since AC1's first branch and AC3 both survive it unmet.

**Readiness deltas this pass**

- `dependencies` → **met**. No open blockers; TKT-157 is Done, TKT-162 is TKT-19's only child, and ADR-025 §D6 hands the scanner durability contract to this lineage — a licence, not a blocker.
- `context_memo` stays **met** but was re-verified rather than trusted: all nine `governingAdrs` resolve to real files at HEAD, and **`governingTests` was missing entirely** from the original bake — now populated with four entries, including the migration four-test set (statement-order / schema / volume / **irreversibility**) that this service enforces and that is discoverable only by failing the gate.
- `scope`, `uncertainties`, `approach`, `first_slice`, `success` remain **open** with `owner: human`, all five now blocked on the *same single decision* rather than on five separate unknowns.
- `approach` now also records the two structural facts above, so the plan drafter inherits them instead of rediscovering them — it reads code, not decision history.

`approach` is deliberately **not** `deferred`. `shaping.md` forbids that escape hatch when a ticket touches an auth surface, and a revocation feed is one: it decides who gets through a door, and the ceiling behaviour *is* the trust boundary.

### ⛔ Gate 1 — held, correctly

Autonomous mode does not replace Gate 1: the agent never self-promotes out of Backlog. The board will refuse the drag while these items are `open`, which is the right outcome — but the question waiting for you is now one decision with a recommendation attached, not an open design space.

**Your move, one of:**

- **(A)** Answer the three staleness sub-questions — then `scope`/`approach`/`first_slice`/`success` all flip in one pass and this ticket becomes claimable as the feed.
- **(B)** Split **Slice B** out as its own ticket to make the hole visible now, and hold TKT-162 for the feed.
- **(C)** Tell me to spawn a spike to measure real venue connectivity if the ceiling is not answerable from the armchair.

<!-- sdlc:stage=backlog kind=readiness -->
### Slice B split out as TKT-269 — TKT-162 keeps the feed

Owner took **option B** from the previous readiness pass. Recording the decision and what moved.

**Split out → [TKT-269]** — *An offline admit of a refunded ticket raises an admission-conflict alarm instead of passing silently.* Shaped to a full 8/8 DoR at creation and sitting in Backlog awaiting Gate 1. It closes **AC1's second branch** (*"or, if it already did, the operator is told through a channel that means this"*) using the alarm class that already exists, `platform.access.admission-conflict.alarm`. It needs no product decision, touches no auth or money surface, and changes nothing a scanner does.

**Retained here** — AC1's **first** branch (a scanner that went offline before a refund and synced after it does not admit the holder) and **AC3** (a bounded, offline-testable revocation feed). Plus, per the previous pass, the new ADR that pushing revocation state toward a gate will need: ADR-025 covers recording after the fact, not distribution.

**Readiness delta:** `first_slice` → **met**. TKT-162's slice is now unambiguous — it is the feed. The remaining `open` items (`scope`, `uncertainties`, `approach`, `success`) are all still gated on the **same single decision**: how stale a scanner's revocation view may be, and whether it fails open or closed past that ceiling.

**Why this ticket does not simply become blocked-by TKT-269.** The two are independent by construction. TKT-269 records that a refunded holder got in; TKT-162 stops it happening. Neither needs the other to ship, and nothing TKT-269 does constrains what the staleness decision can later be — which is exactly why it was safe to split.

### ⛔ Gate 1 — still held, unchanged

The board will keep refusing the drag while four items are `open`, correctly. The question waiting on you is narrower than it was two passes ago but has not been answered: **feed freshness, staleness ceiling, and behaviour at the ceiling** (fail open — today's hole — versus fail closed, which refuses *everyone* on a stale list, not only refunded holders).

One input that would sharpen it, and that isn't in the repo: **how often refunds land during an event, after doors open.** If they cluster days ahead, a once-per-shift pull closes most of the gap and the ceiling barely matters. If same-day refunds are common, the ceiling is the whole design.
